stem: He was effusive in his praise.

stem: The country's politics _______ complex, with more than ten parties competing for power.

stem: The job advertisement stipulates that the applicant _______ three years' experience.
reasoning: Both (a) and (d) are defensible. After verbs of requiring, such as 'stipulate', 'demand' and 'insist', formal English can use the base form of the verb: 'stipulates that the applicant have three years' experience'. 'Must have' states the same requirement with a modal and is the keyed answer, because it is the form most writers use. 'Had' is the wrong tense, and 'shall have' is not used to state a requirement like this.
subtopic: Connector Blanks: Conditionals and Verb Forms

stem: Newspapers have reported heavy flooding in the coastal areas. The damage _______ to be extensive.
reasoning: The damage is the recipient of the expectation, so a present passive is required: 'is expected to be extensive'. 'is expecting' is active (wrong subject role), 'expected' lacks an auxiliary, and 'has been expected' is awkwardly past for a current report.
subtopic: Connector Blanks: Conditionals and Verb Forms

stem: The local bank was robbed by a group of men, _______ were armed.
reasoning: The blank must join a second clause, 'were armed', to the sentence and refer back to 'men'. A relative pronoun does this, and after the preposition 'of' it takes the object form: 'four of whom were armed'. 'Four of these' and 'four of those' are demonstratives, so they would need a full stop or a conjunction before them. 'Four whom' drops the 'of' that links the number to the group.
subtopic: Connector Blanks: Conditionals and Verb Forms

stem: The country _______ several economic changes in the past two decades.
reasoning: Neither option is ideal. 'In the past two decades' describes a period that runs up to now, so the best verb would be 'has undergone', but that is not offered. 'Underwent' is acceptable with a time phrase like 'in the past two decades'. 'Had undergone' is the past perfect, which needs an earlier point in the past to look back from, and this sentence gives none. 'Will be undergoing' is future, and 'have been undergoing' is plural, which does not agree with the singular subject 'the country'. So 'underwent' is the best of the four.
subtopic: Connector Blanks: Conditionals and Verb Forms

stem: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him. He did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.

options.label: C
options.text: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him since he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.

options.label: D
options.text: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him whenever he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.

reasoning: The second sentence gives the reason for the first, so one causal conjunction is needed. 'Since' (c) does this: 'He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him since he did not trust the credentials of the organisation...'. 'As because' (a) piles two conjunctions together. 'Due to' (b) is a preposition and must be followed by a noun, not a clause, so 'due to he did not trust' is ungrammatical. 'Whenever' (d) turns a single refusal into a repeated condition.

stem: He pledged to donate his body parts. He was himself the beneficiary of organ transplantation.

reasoning: The two sentences are linked by cause: having himself received a transplanted organ, he pledged his own organs to help others. 'Because' (b) expresses this. 'Though' (a) and 'but' (d) set up a contrast that the two sentences do not contain, and 'if' (c) makes his own transplant a condition, as if it were uncertain.

'Even he had promised' (b) is ungrammatical, 'if' (c) makes the promise a condition, and 'forever' (d) is an adverb, not a conjunction.
